clause_evidence.reasoning: All 25 samples present well-formed problem statements with clear stem, answer, and options. Each item asks students to solve a specific computational or reference task, directly addressing the foundational action of problem-solving across elapsed time contexts.

Thirteen samples directly ask students to calculate elapsed time between two given moments: they provide start and end times and require the student to determine the duration. An additional twelve samples ask students to work backward from known endpoints and durations to find missing start or end times, all of which implicitly require understanding elapsed time as a core computational concept.

Thirteen samples require students to work with elapsed time measured in minutes, ranging from 5 to 60 minutes. These problems exercise the understanding that time intervals less than one hour can be expressed and calculated in minutes, directly supporting Grade 2 competency to count and calculate minutes as a valid time unit within the hour boundary.

Seven samples require students to calculate or work with elapsed time measured in hours, ranging from 1 to 6 hours. These problems help students understand that time intervals spanning multiple hours can be counted and calculated within a single day, supporting Grade 2 competency with hour-level temporal arithmetic and reasoning about time durations across the school day.

Six samples require students to count or calculate elapsed days within a week, spanning from Thursday-Friday (2 days) to Wednesday-Saturday (4 days). These problems exercise students' understanding of consecutive calendar days and multi-day event duration, directly supporting the Grade 2 competency to count and calculate days of the week as a temporal unit.

Seven samples present timetable visuals (either bus schedules or class schedules) as the primary reference for solving elapsed time problems. Students must extract start and end times from structured table format, a real-world skill directly aligned with the curriculum requirement to work with timetables as a practical context for elapsed time problem-solving.
